title: Paloma and the Smile
premise: Freya Galloway arrives at Hollowmere Primary to replace a teacher who vanished mid-term, and finds a school where one child in every class is quietly 'unaccounted for.' Her compulsive documentation—lesson logs, sleep recordings of the dormitory wing, photographs of the old well behind the chapel—becomes both shield and summons, because the recordings capture a second voice answering questions no one asked aloud. The missing children were taken in 1974 by a staff ritual meant to feed something beneath the well, and the thing has begun refilling. Freya, the caretaker's daughter Wren, and the last surviving teacher of 1974 must return what was taken—the children's names, spoken back into the well at dawn—or become its next entries; Freya gives up her own name to seal it, and the found family she built remembers her only as a warm absence and a notebook full of prayers.
about_author: Isandro Montrose is the pen name of a former boarding-school matron who spent eleven years listening to children talk in their sleep. They write horror about institutions that mistake care for control.

chapters.title: The Intake Form
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. She arrives at fog-bound Hollowmere Primary, signs paperwork that lists her predecessor as 'resigned, effective never,' and meets Wren, the caretaker's feral, watchful daughter. Freya begins her first logbook, documenting everything as ritual comfort. Emotional beat: cautious hope curdling into unease when she counts nineteen desks but eighteen students.

chapters.title: Nineteen Desks
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Teaching her first week, she feels a cold pressure whenever she faces the empty desk, and the children flinch when she says the word 'well' in a geography lesson. The headmaster, Mr. Voss, gently confiscates her class list and returns it with one line inked out. Emotional beat: the loneliness of seeing something everyone else agrees not to see.

chapters.title: What the Night Says
chapters.summary: Freya's POV, interleaved with tape transcripts. She sets a recorder in the dormitory to document her own insomnia and captures a second voice—a child's—answering questions before they're asked. Wren admits children have been going missing since 1974, one per generation, always the invisible ones. Emotional beat: terror braided with fierce protectiveness.

chapters.title: Miss Aldercott Remembers
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Freya and elderly Edith Aldercott, last surviving teacher of 1974. Edith confesses the staff sang the children's names into the well to bind a hunger that predates the school; it worked until the singing stopped. She gives Freya a waterlogged hymnal with nine names torn out. Emotional beat: guilt passed down like an inheritance nobody wants.

chapters.title: The Second Voice Has a Name
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Cross-referencing tapes and parish records, Freya identifies the voice: Thomas Ilbery, taken in 1974, whose desk is hers now. He speaks through the recordings directly to her—'You write us down. Nobody ever wrote us down.' Emotional beat: love arriving in the shape of a haunting; duty beginning to war with belonging.

chapters.title: Voss Knows
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren discovers Mr. Voss's office lined with forty years of intake forms, each with a name inked out—he isn't hiding the taking, he's administering it, believing sacrifice keeps the school alive. He offers Freya tenure in exchange for silence. Emotional beat: the sick recognition that evil here wears a lanyard and means well.

chapters.title: Refilling
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. The well begins to rise, black water climbing the chapel steps; two more children go 'home' overnight and their desks sit cold. Edith dies peacefully mid-sentence, her last word a name. The second voice grows urgent: dawn on the solstice, or the well takes freely. Emotional beat: grief compressing into resolve.

chapters.title: Everything We Kept
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. Freya, Wren, and the remaining children gather every scrap of evidence—tapes, logs, photographs, the hymnal—and the children themselves remember the missing ones aloud, giving them back their favorite things, their jokes, their names. Emotional beat: found family forged in defiance; documentation becomes communion instead of prayer.

chapters.title: Dawn at the Well
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. At solstice dawn they read all nine names into the well; the water fights back, showing each of them what they'd be without the others. Voss arrives to stop them and is taken instead—duty consuming its most faithful servant. Thomas's voice asks Freya for one name more to seal the well shut forever. Emotional beat: climax of love against duty, the choice made before it's spoken.

chapters.title: A Warm Absence
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, one year later. The school is whole, nineteen desks and nineteen children, and no one can quite recall the teacher who left them a notebook full of careful, loving entries signed with a blank. Wren reads it nightly by the sealed well and says thank you anyway. Emotional beat: bittersweet resolution—belonging outlasting the one who bought it.
